title: Warming overwhelms CO2-driven drought mitigation in alpine vegetation on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Droughts have intensified under climate change, threatening ecosystem stability. While rising atmospheric CO2 concentrations may enhance vegetation drought resistance, the net effect remains uncertain amid concurrent warming. Here we combine ecological modeling with multi-source observations to investigate how CO2 and warming jointly regulate vegetation drought responses on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, a sensitive alpine region exposed to escalating drought threats under changing precipitation regimes. Using factorial scenarios to isolate individual forcings, we show that 40-year CO2 rise mitigated drought-induced productivity losses by 5.7 ± 0.9% under constant temperature. However, in the presence of warming, rising CO2 intensifies drought stress by 5.2 ± 0.5%, reflecting increased plant water demand and disrupted regional water supply-demand balance. Permafrost areas experienced the strongest CO2-driven drought alleviation under constant temperature, but also the greatest warming-induced reversal. These findings reveal interacting CO2-warming impacts on alpine vegetation drought responses, highlighting ecological risks for the plateau and other permafrost-dominant regions under future warming. Rising CO₂ levels reduced drought stress on plants on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau over the past four decades, but this benefit is largely cancelled out by warming that increases plant water demand, as revealed by ecological modelling and multi-source observations from 1979 to 2018.
problem: The net effect of rising CO₂ and concurrent warming on vegetation drought resistance is uncertain, as existing studies struggle to disentangle these coupled drivers, and warming may overwhelm the potential drought-mitigating benefits of CO₂.
method: This study combines ecological modeling using factorial scenarios with multi-source observations to disentangle the individual and interactive effects of rising CO₂ and warming on vegetation drought responses on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau.
task: The task is to investigate how rising CO2 and warming jointly regulate vegetation drought responses on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau by combining ecological modeling with multi-source observations.
innovation: This paper reveals that warming has overwhelmed the drought-mitigating benefits of rising CO2 for alpine vegetation on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau by increasing plant water demand and disrupting the regional water supply-demand balance.

As a key regulator of environmental changes across Asia and the Northern Hemisphere, the QTP exerts broad influence on regional and global climate systems¹³. It is not only known as the Asian Water Tower that sustains water resources for over two billion people¹⁴, but also serves as a globally important carbon sink, sequestering around 26.5-33.7 Tg C per year¹⁵. However, this critical carbon-water nexus is now facing unprecedented drought risks.

Here, we investigate the interactions between iCO2, drought stress induced by precipitation deficits, and warming on the QTP. We utilize a multi-source approach, integrating observational data, multi-model simulations from the TRENDY-v12 project (trends and drivers of the regional scale terrestrial sources and sinks of carbon dioxide)33, and scenario-based simulations using a customized dynamic global vegetation model LPJ-GUESS34, driven by fine-resolution climatic data and local parameterization. These simulations apply factorial combinations of CO2 and temperature forcings to isolate their individual and combined effects. We aim to (1) disentangle how iCO2 affects vegetation responses to drought stress across the QTP, (2) determine the role of background warming in modulating this relationship, and (3) quantify how these effects differ

We then customized one of the TRENDY models, the LPJ-GUESS v4.1 model34, specifically for the QTP to disentangle the relative contributions of iCO2 and warming to drought stress mitigation in the region. Building on a well-calibrated foundation34–36 and incorporating enhanced process representations (e.g., soil freeze-thaw processes, daily grass carbon allocation schemes, etc.) as well as locally parameterized plant functional types (PFTs; Figs. S6 and S7; Table S3; see Supplementary Methods for details), the customized model successfully captured both the spatial patterns (Figs. 2 and S8) and temporal trends (Figs. S9 and S10) of vegetation dynamics and eco-hydrological processes, and its performance was further supported by site-level GPP evaluations against flux tower observations (R2 = 0.56, RMSE = 0.05 kg C m¯² month¯¹; Fig. S11).

For model-data comparison, the agreement between simulated and observed GPP was quantified using coefficient of determination (R²), Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (Spearman's p), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean bias error (Bias). R² and p describe the strength and monotonicity of the model-observation relationship, while RMSE and Bias quantify the average and systematic deviations, respectively.

Precipitation data from the Climatic Research Unit gridded Time Series 66 (CRU TS) v4.07 were used to calculate the 12-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI12) and to identify drought and normal years for TRENDY model simulations.

Participating models perform simulations following a common protocol and using a standardized set of driving datasets, including the 0.5° monthly historical climate forcing from CRU TS v4.07 for the period 1901-2022, and annually varying [CO2] from 1700 to 202233.
Soil data were derived from SoilGrids (https://www.isric.org/explore/soilgrids), a global gridded soil information dataset at six standard depth intervals and a spatial resolution of 250 meters.

The soil variables from SoilGrids used in this study were the content of each soil texture (sand, silt, and clay) and bulk density in the 5-15 cm soil layer, which were upscaled to a spatial resolution of 1/8° to avoid potential retrieval errors caused by floating-point precision issues.

The evaluation framework in this study includes GPP, ET, and runoff derived from multi-source observational datasets. Three separate GPP estimates were obtained from (i) a dataset of annual GPP over China's terrestrial ecosystems during 2000-202067,68 (ChinaFLUX20), (ii) a global OCO-2-based solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence dataset69 (GOSIF v2), and (iii) a long-term global GPP dataset based on the near-infrared (NIR) reflectance of vegetation70 (NIRv).
All datasets underwent spatial resampling to a standardized 0.1° grid using bilinear interpolation to ensure dimensional consistency in comparative analyses.
